Vale of White Horse's population increased by around 17,900 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population reached nearly 140,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Vale of White Horse increased by 14.8%, from around 121,000 in 2011 to around 138,900 in 2021.

The population here increased by a greater percentage than the overall population of the South East (7.5%), and by a greater percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Vale of White Horse was home to around 1.7 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 1.5 in 2011. This area was among the lowest 30% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was higher in Vale of White Horse than across the South East

Median age stable in Vale of White Horse

The latest census data also show that the average (median) age remained 41 years in Vale of White Horse between the last two censuses.

This area had a similar average (median) age to the South East as a whole in 2021 (41 years) but a slightly higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 25 to 34 years rose by around 3,600 (an increase of 25.2%), while the number of residents between 16 and 19 years fell by just under 150 (2.3% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 25 and 34 years increased by 1.1 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Vale of White Horse stood out from other areas for housing

The percentage of households in the social rented sector increased in Vale of White Horse, but fell across England.

In Vale of White Horse, the percentage of households in the social rented sector rose from 13.3% in 2011 to 14.3% in 2021, while across England it fell from 17.7% to 17.1%. During the same period, the regional percentage fell from 13.7% to 13.6%.

Private renting in Vale of White Horse increased from 13.6% to 15.7%, while the rate of home ownership decreased from 70.3% to 68.2%.

The rate of social renting in Vale of White Horse increased by 0.9 percentage points

Unpaid care in Vale of White Horse

Vale of White Horse saw the South East's joint largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 7.9% in 2011 to 4.7% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Every local authority area across the South East saw a fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care, as the regional proportion fell from 7.3% to 4.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Vale of White Horse decreased by 3.2 percentage points

National identity in Vale of White Horse

In 2021, 8.0% of Vale of White Horse residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 5.7% in 2011.

In 2021, just over 1 in 40 people (2.7%) identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 1.1% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Vale of White Horse that identified as "British only" increased from 18.2% to 55.8%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater in Vale of White Horse (2.3 percentage points) than across the South East (1.6 percentage points, from 7.1% to 8.7%). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Vale of White Horse increased by 2.3 percentage points

Fewer adults working long hours

In 2021, 11.5% of Vale of White Horse residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked over 49 hours per week. This figure decreased from 14.8% in 2011.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked over 49 hours per week was greater in Vale of White Horse (3.3 percentage points) than across the South East (2.7 percentage points, from 14.6% to 11.9%). Across England, the percentage fell by 2.2 percentage points, from 13.3% to 11.1%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults in employment who worked 49 hours or more in Vale of White Horse decreased by 3.3 percentage points

Religion in Vale of White Horse

In 2021, 41.7% of Vale of White Horse residents reported having "No religion", up from 26.9% in 2011. The rise of 14.8 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Vale of White Horse. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the South East, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 27.7% to 40.2%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 48.6% of people in Vale of White Horse described themselves as Christian (down from 63.3%), while 6.1% did not state their religion (down from 7.4% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Vale of White Horse residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 114,100 Vale of White Horse residents said they were born in England. This represented 82.1% of the local population. The figure has risen from just over 103,300 in 2011, which at the time represented 85.4% of Vale of White Horse's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with around 2,400 Vale of White Horse residents reporting this country of birth (1.7%). This figure has remained relatively unchanged from 2011.

The number of Vale of White Horse residents born in Wales fell from around 2,300 in 2011 (1.9% of the local population) to just under 2,200 in 2021 (1.6%).

In 2021, 82.1% of Vale of White Horse residents reported their country of birth as England

Family in Vale of White Horse

In 2021, 6.3% of Vale of White Horse households included a couple with only non-dependent children. This figure decreased from 6.6% in 2011.

Vale of White Horse saw the South East's largest fall in the percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children.

The percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children in Vale of White Horse decreased by 0.3 percentage points

Health in Vale of White Horse

In 2021, 52.1% of Vale of White Horse residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 51.0% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 34.4% to 34.0%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Vale of White Horse residents describing their health as "very bad" decreased from 0.8% to 0.6%, while those describing their health as "bad" was 2.6% (similar to 2011).

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very bad health in Vale of White Horse decreased by 0.2 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of Vale of White Horse residents aged 16 years and over, 32.0% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 28.3% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in two people (51.9%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 54.9% in 2011. The percentage of adults in Vale of White Horse that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 8.0% to 8.3%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership was greater in Vale of White Horse (3.8 percentage points) than across the South East (2.9 percentage points, from 31.9% to 34.8%). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Vale of White Horse increased by 3.8 percentage points

Change in employment

Of Vale of White Horse residents aged 16 years and over, 61.8% said they were employed (excluding full-time students) in 2021, down from 63.0% in 2011.

In 2021, just under 1 in 50 people (1.9%) said they were unemployed, compared with 2.2% in 2011. The percentage of retired Vale of White Horse residents increased from 22.1% to 22.8%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed in Vale of White Horse (1.2 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the South East (1.3 percentage points, from 59.0% to 57.6%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.8 percentage points, from 56.5% to 55.7%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Vale of White Horse decreased by 1.2 percentage points

Disability in Vale of White Horse

In 2021, 5.0% of Vale of White Horse residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 6.0% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under 1 in 10 people (9.6%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 8.7% in 2011. The proportion of Vale of White Horse residents who were not disabled increased from 85.3% to 85.4%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Vale of White Horse (1.0 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the South East (1.0 percentage points, from 7.2% to 6.2%). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Vale of White Horse decreased by 1.0 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Vale of White Horse

In 2021, 4.0% of Vale of White Horse residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 2.4% in 2011. The 1.5 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the South East, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 5.2% to 7.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 90.8% of people in Vale of White Horse identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 94.9% in 2011), while 2.5% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 1.3% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African" category increased from 1.0% in 2011 to 1.7% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
